processing: Typical of Yunnan sheng: leaf is wok-fixed, rolled and sun-dried, then sold loose or pressed. Nothing documented sets a separate local method.
harvest_season: Spring is usually the prized picking, as elsewhere in Yunnan.
appearance_dry: As with other large-leaf sheng, long dark green leaf with some pale buds.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden yellow when young, as is typical of sheng.
appearance_wet: As with other large-leaf sheng, thick olive-green leaves.
taste_profile: Old-tree tea from this range is described as strong and pure in flavour; finer detail depends on the village and the maker.

brewing.notes: General young sheng approach: quick rinse, short early steeps, and a little patience in the middle steeps.

vintage_note: Usual for regional sheng: sold by harvest year, young, as loose leaf or pressed cakes, with the year and old-tree claim on the wrapper. Aged lots are rarely seen. Ask for the village, since the mountain range is large.
description:
Gaoligong is a long mountain range in western Yunnan near the Myanmar border, and in pu-erh it stands for old-tree tea from the Baoshan side. Think of it as a broad place name, not as one tea garden.

The tea is generally made as other sheng is, so the interest lies with the trees. The range is counted as a significant old-tree resource within the Baoshan area, which also includes Tengchong and Changning gardens.

The flavour is described as strong and pure, though not outstanding beside the three better known regions. Brew it as you would any young sheng, and judge the specific cake rather than the mountain.

Little is written about it, so read grand claims about the oldest or largest tea trees with care. A stated village, year and tree age are more use than the mountain's name.
history: Little is documented about this tea as a named style, and it appears mainly in regional tea guides. It is treated as part of the Baoshan tea area, known mostly for its old-tree resources rather than a famous historic product.
